bullets: A push moves things away, a pull brings them closer, friction slows sliding down, and magnets pull on iron from a distance
slides.heading: Pushes, pulls, friction and magnets
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we meet pushes and pulls, watch friction slow a sliding block, then play with magnets - opposite poles snapping together, like poles pushing apart, and a careful check of which metals a magnet really pulls.

bullets: Tell a push from a pull and explain how friction slows a sliding object down
State what happens when opposite poles and when like poles face each other
Name the metal a magnet reliably pulls and say why not every metal is pulled
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the four goals aloud and tell the class: keep these in mind, because the exit ticket at the end will ask you to sort pushes from pulls, explain friction, predict what two magnets will do, and spot the mistake about magnets and metals.

bullets: A pupil says a magnet will pick up every shiny metal object in the tray
Is that really true for every metal, or only for some of them?
slides.heading: Will a magnet pick up everything shiny?
slides.notes: Pose the claim from scene s4 without the verdict first: ask for a show of hands on whether a magnet pulls every metal, take two or three answers without judging them, and say scene s4 settles this exactly.

bullets: A force is a push or a pull: pushes move things away and pulls bring them closer
Friction is a force too: it rubs against sliding and slows things down
A magnet pulls iron and a few other metals, even without touching them
slides.heading: Forces push, pull, rub and attract
slides.notes: Say this slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: forces change how things move - a push, a pull and friction all need contact, but a magnet can pull iron across a small gap without touching it at all.

bullets: The push arrow shoves the box away across the table
The pull arrow drags the box back closer - same box, opposite force
slides.heading: Push and pull
slides.notes: Narrate the box as it moves in the animation: watch the PUSH label and arrow appear and the box slide away, then the PULL label and arrow appear and the box slide back closer.

bullets: The block slides down the slope, but the rough surface rubs against it
The friction arrow points back up the slope, fighting the slide and slowing the block
slides.heading: Friction slows things down
slides.notes: Follow the block down the slope: point to the rough surface label, then to the friction arrow pushing back against the slide - that rubbing force is why the block slows instead of speeding away.

bullets: Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, marked N and S
When S faces N the magnets pull together and snap with a click
slides.heading: Opposite poles attract
slides.notes: Point to the N and S labels on each magnet: S and N face each other here, so watch the second magnet slide across and snap onto the first - opposite poles attract, even without touching at first.

bullets: Turn one magnet around so N faces N and the magnets push each other apart
A magnet only pulls iron and a few metals - most metals and most things are ignored
slides.heading: Watch out: a magnet does not attract every metal
slides.notes: Hold the warning up first - it is tempting to think every metal jumps to a magnet - then watch N face N and the magnets push apart, and remember the magnet only pulls iron and a few metals, ignoring most things.

bullets: Start with the two magnets apart: the S pole of one faces the N pole of the other
Opposite poles attract, so the loose magnet slides across and snaps onto the first one
slides.heading: Worked example: will these magnets snap together?
slides.notes: Talk through scene s3 slowly and name each step: read the pole labels first, check whether the facing poles are opposite or the same, then predict - opposite poles attract, so the magnets snap together with a click.

bullets: Sort these into pushes and pulls: kicking a ball, dragging a chair towards you, opening a drawer
Predict what happens when two magnets are brought together N to S, then N to N, and explain your answers
slides.heading: Your turn: sort the forces and predict the magnets
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call one pair on each part: press them to name the direction of each force, and to use the words attract for opposite poles and repel for like poles.

bullets: On your own: give one example of a push and one example of a pull
Say what two magnets do when N faces S, and name one metal a magnet does not pull in the way many pupils expect
slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
slides.notes: Collect these before anyone leaves and say: I am looking for a clear push and a clear pull, the attract rule for opposite poles, and care with metals - a magnet only pulls iron and a few metals.
